enchiridion_section-01.originalText: There are things which are within our power, and there are things which are beyond our power. Within our power are opinion, aim, desire, aversion, and, in one word, whatever affairs are our own. Beyond our power are body, property, reputation, office, and, in one word, whatever are not properly our own affairs.
enchiridion_section-01.plainEnglish: Some things are up to you. Some things are not. What's up to you: your opinions, your goals, what you want, and what you want to avoid — basically, anything that is truly your own doing. What's not up to you: your body, your possessions, your reputation, your job title — anything that isn't really your own doing.

enchiridion_section-01.originalText: Now the things within our power are by nature free, unrestricted, unhindered; but those beyond our power are weak, dependent, restricted, alien. Remember, then, that if you attribute freedom to things by nature dependent and take what belongs to others for your own, you will be hindered, you will lament, you will be disturbed, you will find fault both with gods and men. But if you take for your own only that which is your own and view what belongs to others just as it really is, then no one will ever compel you, no one will restrict you; you will find fault with no one, you will accuse no one, you will do nothing against your will; no one will hurt you, you will not have an enemy, nor will you suffer any harm.
enchiridion_section-01.plainEnglish: The things you control are naturally free, unlimited, and unblocked. But the things you don't control are fragile, dependent on others, limited, and foreign to you. Remember this: if you treat dependent things as if they were free, and if you claim other people's stuff as your own, you'll get blocked. You'll complain. You'll get upset. You'll blame both gods and people. But if you only claim what's actually yours, and see other people's stuff for what it really is, then no one can force you to do anything. No one can limit you. You won't blame anyone. You won't accuse anyone. You won't act against your will. No one can hurt you. You won't have enemies. You won't suffer any harm.

enchiridion_section-01.originalText: Aiming, therefore, at such great things, remember that you must not allow yourself any inclination, however slight, toward the attainment of the others; but that you must entirely quit some of them, and for the present postpone the rest. But if you would have these, and possess power and wealth likewise, you may miss the latter in seeking the former; and you will certainly fail of that by which alone happiness and freedom are procured.
enchiridion_section-01.plainEnglish: Since you're aiming for such important things, don't let yourself want other things even a little bit. You must completely give up some desires. Put others on hold for now. If you try to have both — these great things and also power and wealth — you'll probably lose the power and wealth while chasing the great things. And you'll definitely lose the only things that actually bring happiness and freedom.

enchiridion_section-01.originalText: Seek at once, therefore, to be able to say to every unpleasing semblance, "You are but a semblance and by no means the real thing." And then examine it by those rules which you have; and first and chiefly by this: whether it concerns the things which are within our own power or those which are not; and if it concerns anything beyond our power, be prepared to say that it is nothing to you.
enchiridion_section-01.plainEnglish: Start right now. When something looks bad to you, tell it: "You're just an appearance. You're not the real thing." Then test it with your rules. Ask this first: Does this involve something I control or something I don't? If it's something beyond your control, be ready to say it means nothing to you.

enchiridion_section-02.originalText:
Remember that desire demands the attainment of that of which you are
desirous; and aversion demands the avoidance of that to which you are
averse; that he who fails of the object of his desires is disappointed;
and he who incurs the object of his aversion is wretched. If, then, you
shun only those undesirable things which you can control, you will never
incur anything which you shun; but if you shun sickness, or death, or
poverty, you will run the risk of wretchedness. Remove [the habit of]
aversion, then, from all things that are not within our power, and apply
it to things undesirable which are within our power. But for the present,
altogether restrain desire; for if you desire any of the things not
within our own power, you must necessarily be disappointed; and you are
not yet secure of those which are within our power, and so are legitimate
objects of desire. Where it is practically necessary for you to pursue or
avoid anything, do even this with discretion and gentleness and
moderation.
enchiridion_section-02.plainEnglish: Remember how desire and aversion work. When you want something, you demand to get it. When you hate something, you demand to avoid it. If you don't get what you want, you're disappointed. If you get what you hate, you're miserable. So only avoid things you can actually control. You'll never face anything you're trying to avoid. But if you try to avoid sickness, death, or poverty, you're setting yourself up for misery. Stop being averse to things outside your power. Save your aversion for bad things you can control. For now, hold back on wanting things altogether. If you want something outside your control, you'll definitely be let down. And you're not even secure with the things you can control yet — the things it's actually reasonable to want. When you absolutely must pursue or avoid something, do it carefully and gently and in moderation.

enchiridion_section-03.originalText:
With regard to whatever objects either delight the mind or contribute to
use or are tenderly beloved, remind yourself of what nature they are,
beginning with the merest trifles: if you have a favorite cup, that it is
but a cup of which you are fond of—for thus, if it is broken, you can
bear it; if you embrace your child or your wife, that you embrace a
mortal—and thus, if either of them dies, you can bear it.
enchiridion_section-03.plainEnglish: For anything that brings you joy, serves a purpose, or that you love dearly, remind yourself what it really is. Start with small things. If you have a favorite cup, tell yourself: "This is just a cup that I happen to like." That way, if it breaks, you can handle it. If you hug your child or your spouse, remember: "I'm hugging someone who will die someday." That way, if they die, you can bear it.

enchiridion_section-04.originalText:
When you set about any action, remind yourself of what nature the action
is. If you are going to bathe, represent to yourself the incidents usual
in the bath—some persons pouring out, others pushing in, others scolding,
others pilfering. And thus you will more safely go about this action if
you say to yourself, “I will now go to bathe and keep my own will in
harmony with nature.” And so with regard to every other action. For thus,
if any impediment arises in bathing, you will be able to say, “It was not
only to bathe that I desired, but to keep my will in harmony with nature;
and I shall not keep it thus if I am out of humor at things that happen.”
enchiridion_section-04.plainEnglish: Before you do anything, remind yourself what you're actually getting into. If you're going to take a bath, picture what usually happens at the baths — some people splashing water everywhere, others pushing to get in, others complaining, others stealing your stuff. You'll handle it better if you tell yourself, "I'm going to bathe and keep my attitude in line with how things naturally are." Do this with everything you do. That way, if something goes wrong while you're bathing, you can say, "I didn't just want to get clean. I wanted to keep my attitude right. And I won't do that if I get angry about normal stuff that happens."

enchiridion_section-05.originalText:
Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of
things. Thus death is nothing terrible, else it would have appeared so to
Socrates. But the terror consists in our notion of death, that it is
terrible. When, therefore, we are hindered or disturbed, or grieved, let
us never impute it to others, but to ourselves—that is, to our own views.
It is the action of an uninstructed person to reproach others for his own
misfortunes; of one entering upon instruction, to reproach himself; and
one perfectly instructed, to reproach neither others nor himself.
enchiridion_section-05.plainEnglish: It's not things that upset you. It's how you think about them. Death, for example, is not frightening on its own. If it were, Socrates would have been afraid of it. The fear comes from our belief that death is terrible. So when you feel blocked, upset, or sad, don't blame other people. Blame yourself — blame your own thoughts. An ignorant person blames others for his problems. A student blames himself. A wise person blames no one.

enchiridion_section-06.originalText:
Be not elated at any excellence not your own. If a horse should be
elated, and say, “I am handsome,” it might be endurable. But when you are
elated and say, “I have a handsome horse,” know that you are elated only
on the merit of the horse. What then is your own? The use of the
phenomena of existence. So that when you are in harmony with nature in
this respect, you will be elated with some reason; for you will be elated
at some good of your own.
enchiridion_section-06.plainEnglish: Don't get excited about things that aren't really yours. If a horse got excited and said, "I'm beautiful," that would make sense. But when you get excited and say, "I have a beautiful horse," you're getting excited about something that belongs to the horse, not you. So what actually belongs to you? How you handle what happens to you. When you do that well — when you work with life instead of against it — then you have a real reason to be proud. You're proud of something that's actually yours.

enchiridion_section-07.originalText:
As in a voyage, when the ship is at anchor, if you go on shore to get
water, you may amuse yourself with picking up a shellfish or a truffle in
your way, but your thoughts ought to be bent toward the ship, and
perpetually attentive, lest the captain should call, and then you must
leave all these things, that you may not have to be carried on board the
vessel, bound like a sheep; thus likewise in life, if, instead of a
truffle or shellfish, such a thing as a wife or a child be granted you,
there is no objection; but if the captain calls, run to the ship, leave
all these things, and never look behind. But if you are old, never go far
from the ship, lest you should be missing when called for.
enchiridion_section-07.plainEnglish: Think of life like a sea voyage. When your ship drops anchor, you can go ashore to get water. You might pick up a shell or find a mushroom along the way — that's fine. But keep your mind on the ship. Stay alert. If the captain calls, you have to drop everything and get back on board. You don't want to be dragged onto the ship tied up like an animal. Life works the same way. Instead of shells and mushrooms, you might be given a spouse or children. That's fine too. But when the captain calls, run to the ship. Leave everything behind. Don't look back. And if you're getting old, don't wander far from the ship. You don't want to miss the call.

enchiridion_section-08.originalText:
Demand not that events should happen as you wish; but wish them to happen
as they do happen, and you will go on well.
enchiridion_section-08.plainEnglish: Don't demand that things happen the way you want them to. Instead, want them to happen the way they do happen. Then you'll be fine.

enchiridion_section-09.originalText:
Sickness is an impediment to the body, but not to the will unless itself
pleases. Lameness is an impediment to the leg, but not to the will; and
say this to yourself with regard to everything that happens. For you will
find it to be an impediment to something else, but not truly to yourself.
enchiridion_section-09.plainEnglish: Being sick limits your body, but not your will — unless you let it. Being lame limits your leg, but not your will. Tell yourself this about everything that happens to you. You'll find that these things limit something else, but not your true self.

enchiridion_section-10.originalText:
Upon every accident, remember to turn toward yourself and inquire what
faculty you have for its use. If you encounter a handsome person, you
will find continence the faculty needed; if pain, then fortitude; if
reviling, then patience. And when thus habituated, the phenomena of
existence will not overwhelm you.
enchiridion_section-10.plainEnglish: When anything happens to you, stop and ask yourself: what strength do I have to handle this? If you meet an attractive person, you'll need self-control. If you feel pain, you'll need courage. If someone insults you, you'll need patience. Practice this habit, and life's events won't overwhelm you.

enchiridion_section-11.originalText:
Never say of anything, “I have lost it,” but, “I have restored it.” Has
your child died? It is restored. Has your wife died? She is restored. Has
your estate been taken away? That likewise is restored. “But it was a bad
man who took it.” What is it to you by whose hands he who gave it has
demanded it again? While he permits you to possess it, hold it as
something not your own, as do travelers at an inn.
enchiridion_section-11.plainEnglish: Never say 'I lost it.' Say 'I gave it back.' Did your child die? You gave them back. Did your wife die? You gave her back. Did someone take your property? You gave that back too. 'But the person who took it was evil.' So what? Why does it matter whose hands the original giver used to take it back? While you're allowed to have these things, treat them like borrowed items. Think of yourself as a traveler staying at an inn.

enchiridion_section-12.originalText:
If you would improve, lay aside such reasonings as these: “If I neglect
my affairs, I shall not have a maintenance; if I do not punish my
servant, he will be good for nothing.” For it were better to die of
hunger, exempt from grief and fear, than to live in affluence with
perturbation; and it is better that your servant should be bad than you
unhappy.

Begin therefore with little things. Is a little oil spilled or a little
wine stolen? Say to yourself, “This is the price paid for peace and
tranquillity; and nothing is to be had for nothing.” And when you call
your servant, consider that it is possible he may not come at your call;
or, if he does, that he may not do what you wish. But it is not at all
desirable for him, and very undesirable for you, that it should be in his
power to cause you any disturbance.
enchiridion_section-12.plainEnglish:
If you want to get better, stop thinking like this: "If I don't take care of my business, I'll go broke. If I don't punish my servant, he'll be worthless." It's better to starve to death without worry and fear than to be rich and miserable. It's better for your servant to be bad than for you to be unhappy.

So start with small things. Did someone spill a little oil or steal some wine? Tell yourself, "This is what I pay for peace of mind. Nothing comes free." When you call your servant, remember he might not come. Or if he does come, he might not do what you want. But it's not good for him to have that power over you — and it's terrible for you to let him disturb your peace.

enchiridion_section-13.originalText:
If you would improve, be content to be thought foolish and dull with
regard to externals. Do not desire to be thought to know anything; and
though you should appear to others to be somebody, distrust yourself. For
be assured, it is not easy at once to keep your will in harmony with
nature and to secure externals; but while you are absorbed in the one,
you must of necessity neglect the other.
enchiridion_section-13.plainEnglish: If you want to get better, be okay with people thinking you're clueless about external things. Don't try to look like you know everything. Even if others think you're important, don't trust that feeling. Here's the truth: you can't focus on both living according to nature and chasing external things at the same time. When you're absorbed in one, you'll necessarily ignore the other.

enchiridion_section-14.originalText:
If you wish your children and your wife and your friends to live forever,
you are foolish, for you wish things to be in your power which are not
so, and what belongs to others to be your own. So likewise, if you wish
your servant to be without fault, you are foolish, for you wish vice not
to be vice but something else. But if you wish not to be disappointed in
your desires, that is in your own power. Exercise, therefore, what is in
your power. A man’s master is he who is able to confer or remove whatever
that man seeks or shuns. Whoever then would be free, let him wish
nothing, let him decline nothing, which depends on others; else he must
necessarily be a slave.
enchiridion_section-14.plainEnglish: If you want your children, wife, and friends to live forever, you're being foolish. You're wishing for control over things that aren't up to you. You're trying to make other people's business your business. Same thing if you expect your employee to never make mistakes. You're being foolish. You're wishing that human flaws weren't human flaws. But if you want to avoid disappointment in what you desire — that's actually up to you. So work on what you can control. Here's the truth: whoever can give you what you want or take it away is your master. So if you want to be free, don't pin your hopes on things that depend on other people. Don't fear things that depend on other people either. Otherwise, you'll always be someone's slave.

enchiridion_section-15.originalText:
Remember that you must behave as at a banquet. Is anything brought round
to you? Put out your hand and take a moderate share. Does it pass by you?
Do not stop it. Is it not yet come? Do not yearn in desire toward it, but
wait till it reaches you. So with regard to children, wife, office,
riches; and you will some time or other be worthy to feast with the gods.
And if you do not so much as take the things which are set before you,
but are able even to forego them, then you will not only be worthy to
feast with the gods, but to rule with them also. For, by thus doing,
Diogenes and Heraclitus, and others like them, deservedly became divine,
and were so recognized.
enchiridion_section-15.plainEnglish: Remember that you must behave like you're at a dinner party. Is something passed around to you? Reach out and take a reasonable portion. Does it pass you by? Don't grab for it. Hasn't it come to you yet? Don't sit there craving it. Just wait until it reaches you. Think this way about children, your spouse, your job, and money. If you do this, you'll eventually be worthy to dine with the gods. And if you can not only avoid grabbing at things, but actually turn down what's offered to you, then you won't just be worthy to dine with the gods — you'll be worthy to rule alongside them. This is how Diogenes and Heraclitus, and others like them, rightfully became godlike and were recognized as such.

enchiridion_section-16.originalText:
When you see anyone weeping for grief, either that his son has gone
abroad or that he has suffered in his affairs, take care not to be
overcome by the apparent evil, but discriminate and be ready to say,
“What hurts this man is not this occurrence itself—for another man might
not be hurt by it—but the view he chooses to take of it.” As far as
conversation goes, however, do not disdain to accommodate yourself to him
and, if need be, to groan with him. Take heed, however, not to groan
inwardly, too.
enchiridion_section-16.plainEnglish: When you see someone crying because their child moved away or they lost money, don't get swept up in their drama. Stay clear-headed and remember: "What's hurting this person isn't what actually happened — someone else might not be bothered by the same thing — but how they're choosing to see it." That said, don't be a jerk about it. Go ahead and comfort them. Sympathize with them if you need to. Just don't actually buy into their upset yourself.

enchiridion_section-17.originalText:
Remember that you are an actor in a drama of such sort as the Author
chooses—if short, then in a short one; if long, then in a long one. If it
be his pleasure that you should enact a poor man, or a cripple, or a
ruler, or a private citizen, see that you act it well. For this is your
business—to act well the given part, but to choose it belongs to another.
enchiridion_section-17.plainEnglish: Remember that you're an actor in a play. The Author decides what kind of play it is — short or long. If the Author wants you to play a poor person, a disabled person, a leader, or an ordinary citizen, make sure you play that role well. This is your job — to act well in whatever part you're given. Choosing the part belongs to someone else.

enchiridion_section-18.originalText:
When a raven happens to croak unluckily, be not overcome by appearances,
but discriminate and say, “Nothing is portended to _me_, either to my
paltry body, or property, or reputation, or children, or wife. But to
_me_ all portents are lucky if I will. For whatsoever happens, it belongs
to me to derive advantage therefrom.”
enchiridion_section-18.plainEnglish: When a raven croaks at a bad time, don't let appearances fool you. Think clearly and say, "This means nothing for me — not for my body, my possessions, my reputation, my children, or my wife. For me, all omens are good omens if I choose to see them that way. Whatever happens, I can find a way to benefit from it."

enchiridion_section-19.originalText:
You can be unconquerable if you enter into no combat in which it is not
in your own power to conquer. When, therefore, you see anyone eminent in
honors or power, or in high esteem on any other account, take heed not to
be bewildered by appearances and to pronounce him happy; for if the
essence of good consists in things within our own power, there will be no
room for envy or emulation. But, for your part, do not desire to be a
general, or a senator, or a consul, but to be free; and the only way to
this is a disregard of things which lie not within our own power.
enchiridion_section-19.plainEnglish: You can't be defeated if you only fight battles you can actually win. So when you see someone with high honors, power, or fame, don't be fooled by appearances. Don't call them happy. If what's truly good comes from things you control, then there's no reason to envy or compete with them. Don't try to become a general, senator, or consul. Try to become free. The only way to do that is to stop caring about things you can't control.

enchiridion_section-20.originalText:
Remember that it is not he who gives abuse or blows, who affronts, but
the view we take of these things as insulting. When, therefore, anyone
provokes you, be assured that it is your own opinion which provokes you.
Try, therefore, in the first place, not to be bewildered by appearances.
For if you once gain time and respite, you will more easily command
yourself.
enchiridion_section-20.plainEnglish: Remember: it's not the person who insults you or hits you that offends you. It's how you see these things as offensive. So when someone provokes you, know that it's your own thoughts that are provoking you. First, try not to get swept up by what seems to be happening. If you can pause and give yourself a moment, you'll have much better control over yourself.

enchiridion_section-21.originalText:
Let death and exile, and all other things which appear terrible, be daily
before your eyes, but death chiefly; and you will never entertain an
abject thought, nor too eagerly covet anything.
enchiridion_section-21.plainEnglish: Think about death every day. Think about exile and all the other things that seem scary. But especially death. Do this and you'll never have weak thoughts or desperately want things you shouldn't.

enchiridion_section-22.originalText:
If you have an earnest desire toward philosophy, prepare yourself from
the very first to have the multitude laugh and sneer, and say, “He is
returned to us a philosopher all at once”; and, “Whence this supercilious
look?” Now, for your part, do not have a supercilious look indeed, but
keep steadily to those things which appear best to you, as one appointed
by God to this particular station. For remember that, if you are
persistent, those very persons who at first ridiculed will afterwards
admire you. But if you are conquered by them, you will incur a double
ridicule.
enchiridion_section-22.plainEnglish: If you truly want to study philosophy, get ready for people to mock you from day one. They'll laugh and say, "Look who thinks he's a philosopher now!" and "Where did this arrogant attitude come from?" Don't actually be arrogant. But stick to what seems right to you, like someone God assigned to this specific role. Remember: if you stay committed, the same people who mocked you at first will later respect you. But if you give in to them, you'll be twice as ridiculous.

enchiridion_section-23.originalText:
If you ever happen to turn your attention to externals, for the pleasure
of anyone, be assured that you have ruined your scheme of life. Be
content, then, in everything, with being a philosopher; and if you wish
to seem so likewise to anyone, appear so to yourself, and it will suffice
you.
enchiridion_section-23.plainEnglish: If you ever focus on external things to please someone else, you've wrecked your whole approach to life. Be satisfied with being a philosopher in everything you do. If you want to appear wise to others, just appear wise to yourself. That's enough.

enchiridion_section-24.originalText: Let not such considerations as these distress you: "I shall live in discredit and be nobody anywhere." For if discredit be an evil, you can no more be involved in evil through another than in baseness. Is it any business of yours, then, to get power or to be admitted to an entertainment? By no means. How then, after all, is this discredit? And how it is true that you will be nobody anywhere when you ought to be somebody in those things only which are within your own power, in which you may be of the greatest consequence?
enchiridion_section-24.plainEnglish: Don't let thoughts like this upset you: "People will think badly of me and I'll be a nobody." If having a bad reputation is truly bad, then you can't be harmed by what someone else does any more than you can be made immoral by them. Is it your job to gain power or get invited to parties? Not at all. So how is this really disgrace? And how are you really a nobody when you should only matter in the things that are actually up to you — the things where you can have real importance?

enchiridion_section-24.originalText: "But my friends will be unassisted." What do you mean by "unassisted"? They will not have money from you, nor will you make them Roman citizens. Who told you, then, that these are among the things within our own power, and not rather the affairs of others? And who can give to another the things which he himself has not? "Well, but get them, then, that we too may have a share." If I can get them with the preservation of my own honor and fidelity and self-respect, show me the way and I will get them; but if you require me to lose my own proper good, that you may gain what is no good, consider how unreasonable and foolish you are. Besides, which would you rather have, a sum of money or a faithful and honorable friend? Rather assist me, then, to gain this character than require me to do those things by which I may lose it.
enchiridion_section-24.plainEnglish: "But my friends won't get help." What do you mean by "help"? They won't get money from you, and you won't make them Roman citizens. Who told you that these things are up to you anyway? They're other people's business. How can you give someone what you don't even have yourself? "Well, go get those things so we can benefit too." If I can get them without losing my honor, integrity, and self-respect, show me how and I'll do it. But if you're asking me to sacrifice my character so you can gain something worthless, think about how foolish that is. Besides, what would you rather have — some money or a loyal, honorable friend? Help me build that kind of character instead of asking me to destroy it.

enchiridion_section-24.originalText: Well, but my country, say you, as far as depends upon me, will be unassisted. Here, again, what assistance is this you mean? It will not have porticos nor baths of your providing? And what signifies that? Why, neither does a smith provide it with shoes, nor a shoemaker with arms. It is enough if everyone fully performs his own proper business. And were you to supply it with another faithful and honorable citizen, would not he be of use to it? Yes. Therefore neither are you yourself useless to it. "What place, then," say you, "shall I hold in the state?" Whatever you can hold with the preservation of your fidelity and honor. But if, by desiring to be useful to that, you lose these, how can you serve your country when you have become faithless and shameless?
enchiridion_section-24.plainEnglish: "But my country won't get any help from me," you say. What kind of help do you mean? Your country won't get fancy buildings or public baths from you? So what? A blacksmith doesn't provide the country with shoes. A shoemaker doesn't provide it with weapons. It's enough if everyone does their own job well. If you gave your country another honest and honorable citizen, wouldn't that be useful? Yes. So you're not useless to your country either. "But what position will I hold in the government?" you ask. Whatever position you can hold while keeping your integrity and honor. If you lose those things by trying to be useful, how can you serve your country once you've become untrustworthy and shameless?

enchiridion_section-25.originalText:
Is anyone preferred before you at an entertainment, or in courtesies, or
in confidential intercourse? If these things are good, you ought to
rejoice that he has them; and if they are evil, do not be grieved that
you have them not. And remember that you cannot be permitted to rival
others in externals without using the same means to obtain them. For how
can he who will not haunt the door of any man, will not attend him, will
not praise him, have an equal share with him who does these things? You
are unjust, then, and unreasonable if you are unwilling to pay the price
for which these things are sold, and would have them for nothing. For how
much are lettuces sold? An obulus, for instance.
enchiridion_section-25.plainEnglish: Does someone get invited to better parties than you? Do they get more respect or closer friendships? If these things are actually good, you should be happy for them. If they're bad, don't feel sorry that you don't have them. Remember: you can't compete with others for external rewards without doing what they do to get them. How can someone who won't visit important people, attend their events, or flatter them expect the same treatment as someone who does all that? You're being unfair and unreasonable if you want these rewards without paying their price. It's like wanting lettuce for free when it costs money.

enchiridion_section-25.originalText:
If another, then, paying
an obulus, takes the lettuces, and you, not paying it, go without them,
do not imagine that he has gained any advantage over you. For as he has
the lettuces, so you have the obulus which you did not give. So, in the
present case, you have not been invited to such a person’s entertainment
because you have not paid him the price for which a supper is sold. It is
sold for praise; it is sold for attendance. Give him, then, the value if
it be for your advantage. But if you would at the same time not pay the
one, and yet receive the other, you are unreasonable and foolish. Have
you nothing, then, in place of the supper? Yes, indeed, you have—not to
praise him whom you do not like to praise; not to bear the insolence of
his lackeys.
enchiridion_section-25.plainEnglish: If someone else pays a coin for lettuce and takes it, while you don't pay and go without, don't think they got a better deal than you. They have the lettuce, but you still have your coin. Same thing here. You weren't invited to that person's dinner party because you didn't pay the price that dinner invitations cost. They're sold for flattery and attention. So pay up if it's worth it to you. But if you want to keep your dignity and still get invited, you're being unreasonable and foolish. Don't you get anything instead of the dinner? Of course you do. You don't have to praise someone you don't respect. You don't have to put up with their servants treating you badly.

enchiridion_section-26.originalText:
The will of nature may be learned from things upon which we are all
agreed. As when our neighbor’s boy has broken a cup, or the like, we are
ready at once to say, “These are casualties that will happen”; be
assured, then, that when your own cup is likewise broken, you ought to be
affected just as when another’s cup was broken. Now apply this to greater
things. Is the child or wife of another dead? There is no one who would
not say, “This is an accident of mortality.” But if anyone’s own child
happens to die, it is immediately, “Alas! how wretched am I!” It should
be always remembered how we are affected on hearing the same thing
concerning others.
enchiridion_section-26.plainEnglish: You can learn what's natural by looking at things everyone agrees on. When your neighbor's kid breaks a cup, you're quick to say, "These things happen." So when your own cup breaks, you should react the same way you did when someone else's cup broke. Now apply this to bigger things. When someone else's child or spouse dies, everyone says, "That's just part of life." But when your own child dies, suddenly it's "Oh no! How terrible for me!" Always remember how you react when you hear the same news about other people.

enchiridion_section-27.originalText:
As a mark[1] is not set up for the sake of missing the aim, so neither
does the nature of evil exist in the world.
enchiridion_section-27.plainEnglish: Just as a target isn't set up so you can miss it, evil doesn't exist as part of the natural order of the world.

enchiridion_section-28.originalText:
If a person had delivered up your body to some passer-by, you would
certainly be angry. And do you feel no shame in delivering up your own
mind to any reviler, to be disconcerted and confounded?
enchiridion_section-28.plainEnglish: If someone handed your body over to a stranger, you'd be furious. So why aren't you ashamed when you hand your mind over to anyone who insults you, letting them upset and confuse you?

enchiridion_section-29.originalText: In every affair consider what precedes and what follows, and then undertake it. Otherwise you will begin with spirit, indeed, careless of the consequences, and when these are developed, you will shamefully desist. "I would conquer at the Olympic Games." But consider what precedes and what follows, and then, if it be for your advantage, engage in the affair. You must conform to rules, submit to a diet, refrain from dainties; exercise your body, whether you choose it or not, at a stated hour, in heat and cold; you must drink no cold water, and sometimes no wine—in a word, you must give yourself up to your trainer as to a physician. Then, in the combat, you may be thrown into a ditch, dislocate your arm, turn your ankle, swallow an abundance of dust, receive stripes [for negligence], and, after all, lose the victory. When you have reckoned up all this, if your inclination still holds, set about the combat.
enchiridion_section-29.plainEnglish: Before you start anything, think about what comes before and what comes after. Then decide if you want to do it. Otherwise you'll start with excitement, ignore the consequences, and when reality hits, you'll quit in shame. "I want to win at the Olympics." Fine. But think about what that really means. If it's worth it, then go for it. You'll have to follow strict rules. You'll have to diet and give up treats. You'll have to train your body at set times, whether you feel like it or not, in heat and cold. No cold water. Sometimes no wine. You'll have to surrender completely to your trainer like a patient to a doctor. Then in the actual competition, you might get thrown in a ditch, dislocate your arm, twist your ankle, swallow a mouthful of dust, get beaten up, and still lose. Once you've counted up all of this, if you still want it, then start training.

enchiridion_section-29.originalText: Otherwise, take notice, you will behave like children who sometimes play wrestlers, sometimes gladiators, sometimes blow a trumpet, and sometimes act a tragedy, when they happen to have seen and admired these shows. Thus you too will be at one time a wrestler, and another a gladiator; now a philosopher, now an orator; but nothing in earnest. Like an ape you mimic all you see, and one thing after another is sure to please you, but is out of favor as soon as it becomes familiar. For you have never entered upon anything considerately; nor after having surveyed and tested the whole matter, but carelessly, and with a halfway zeal.
enchiridion_section-29.plainEnglish: Without proper planning, you'll act like children playing games. Kids pretend to be wrestlers, then gladiators, then trumpet players, then actors — copying whatever show impressed them last. You'll do the same thing. One day you'll be a wrestler, the next a gladiator. Now a philosopher, now a public speaker. But you won't take any of it seriously. Like a monkey, you'll copy everything you see. Each new thing will excite you until it becomes boring. Why? Because you never think things through. You never study the whole situation and test it properly. You just jump in carelessly with half-hearted effort.

enchiridion_section-29.originalText: Thus some, when they have seen a philosopher and heard a man speaking like Euphrates[3]—though, indeed, who can speak like him?—have a mind to be philosophers, too. Consider first, man, what the matter is, and what your own nature is able to bear. If you would be a wrestler, consider your shoulders, your back, your thighs; for different persons are made for different things. Do you think that you can act as you do and be a philosopher, that you can eat, drink, be angry, be discontented, as you are now? You must watch, you must labor, you must get the better of certain appetites, must quit your acquaintances, be despised by your servant, be laughed at by those you meet; come off worse than others in everything—in offices, in honors, before tribunals.
enchiridion_section-29.plainEnglish: Some people hear a philosopher speak — someone like Euphrates, though really, who can speak like him? — and suddenly they want to be philosophers too. But first, think about what this actually means. Consider what you're capable of. If you wanted to be a wrestler, you'd check your shoulders, your back, your thighs. Different people are built for different things. Do you think you can keep living exactly as you do now and be a philosopher? Can you keep eating, drinking, getting angry, and complaining like you always have? You'll have to stay alert. You'll have to work hard. You'll have to control certain desires. You'll have to leave your friends behind. Your servants will look down on you. People will laugh at you. You'll lose out to others in everything — jobs, honors, court cases.

enchiridion_section-29.originalText: When you have fully considered all these things, approach, if you please—that is, if, by parting with them, you have a mind to purchase serenity, freedom, and tranquillity. If not, do not come hither; do not, like children, be now a philosopher, then a publican, then an orator, and then one of Caesar's officers. These things are not consistent. You must be one man, either good or bad. You must cultivate either your own reason or else externals; apply yourself either to things within or without you—that is, be either a philosopher or one of the mob.
enchiridion_section-29.plainEnglish: Think about all this carefully. Then decide. If you're willing to give up those things to gain peace, freedom, and calm — go ahead and start. If not, don't bother. Don't be like children who play at being different things — first a philosopher, then a tax collector, then a speaker, then one of Caesar's officials. These roles don't mix. You must be one person, either good or bad. You must develop either your own thinking or chase external things. Focus either on what's within you or what's outside you. Be either a philosopher or just another person in the crowd.

enchiridion_section-30.originalText:
Duties are universally measured by relations. Is a certain man your
father? In this are implied taking care of him, submitting to him in all
things, patiently receiving his reproaches, his correction. But he is a
bad father. Is your natural tie, then, to a _good_ father? No, but to a
father. Is a brother unjust? Well, preserve your own just relation toward
him. Consider not what _he_ does, but what _you_ are to do to keep your
own will in a state conformable to nature, for another cannot hurt you
unless you please. You will then be hurt when you consent to be hurt. In
this manner, therefore, if you accustom yourself to contemplate the
relations of neighbor, citizen, commander, you can deduce from each the
corresponding duties.
enchiridion_section-30.plainEnglish: Your duties come from your relationships. Is someone your father? Then you should care for him, respect him, and accept his criticism patiently — even if he's a bad father. Your natural bond isn't to a good father. It's to your father, period. Is your brother unfair? Keep treating him fairly anyway. Don't focus on what he does. Focus on what you need to do to stay true to your nature. No one can hurt you unless you let them. You only get hurt when you choose to be hurt. Use this same approach with neighbors, fellow citizens, and leaders. Each relationship shows you what your duties are.

enchiridion_section-31.originalText: Be assured that the essence of piety toward the gods lies in this—to form right opinions concerning them, as existing and as governing the universe justly and well. And fix yourself in this resolution, to obey them, and yield to them, and willingly follow them amidst all events, as being ruled by the most perfect wisdom. For thus you will never find fault with the gods, nor accuse them of neglecting you.
enchiridion_section-31.plainEnglish: True devotion to the gods comes down to this: think correctly about them. They exist. They run the universe justly and well. Commit to obeying them, yielding to them, and following them willingly through whatever happens. They rule with perfect wisdom. If you do this, you'll never blame the gods or accuse them of abandoning you.

enchiridion_section-31.originalText: And it is not possible for this to be affected in any other way than by withdrawing yourself from things which are not within our own power, and by making good or evil to consist only in those which are. For if you suppose any other things to be either good or evil, it is inevitable that, when you are disappointed of what you wish or incur what you would avoid, you should reproach and blame their authors.
enchiridion_section-31.plainEnglish: You can't achieve this piety any other way. You must stop caring about things outside your control. You must decide that only your own choices are truly good or bad. If you think other things are good or evil, you'll inevitably get upset when you don't get what you want or when bad things happen to you. Then you'll blame the gods.

enchiridion_section-31.originalText: For every creature is naturally formed to flee and abhor things that appear hurtful and that which causes them; and to pursue and admire those which appear beneficial and that which causes them. It is impracticable, then, that one who supposes himself to be hurt should rejoice in the person who, as he thinks, hurts him, just as it is impossible to rejoice in the hurt itself. Hence, also, a father is reviled by his son when he does not impart the things which seem to be good; and this made Polynices and Eteocles mutually enemies—that empire seemed good to both. On this account the husbandman reviles the gods; [and so do] the sailor, the merchant, or those who have lost wife or child. For where our interest is, there, too, is piety directed.
enchiridion_section-31.plainEnglish: Every living thing naturally runs from what seems harmful and seeks what seems beneficial. So it's impossible for someone who thinks they've been hurt to feel good about the person they think hurt them. You can't enjoy being hurt. This is why a father gets cursed by his son when he doesn't give him what the son thinks is good. This is what made Polynices and Eteocles enemies — they both thought power was good. This is why farmers curse the gods when crops fail. So do sailors, merchants, and people who lose their spouse or children. We worship whatever we think serves our interests.

enchiridion_section-31.originalText: So that whoever is careful to regulate his desires and aversions as he ought is thus made careful of piety likewise. But it also becomes incumbent on everyone to offer libations and sacrifices and first fruits, according to the customs of his country, purely, and not heedlessly nor negligently; not avariciously, nor yet extravagantly.
enchiridion_section-31.plainEnglish: So if you control your desires and aversions properly, you'll naturally respect the gods too. But you should also follow your country's religious customs. Offer sacrifices and first fruits. Do it with a pure heart. Don't be careless or lazy about it. Don't be cheap, but don't go overboard either.

enchiridion_section-32.originalText: When you have recourse to divination, remember that you know not what the event will be, and you come to learn it of the diviner; but of what nature it is you knew before coming; at least, if you are of philosophic mind. For if it is among the things not within our own power, it can by no means be either good or evil. Do not, therefore, bring with you to the diviner either desire or aversion—else you will approach him trembling—but first clearly understand that every event is indifferent and nothing to _you_, of whatever sort it may be; for it will be in your power to make a right use of it, and this no one can hinder. Then come with confidence to the gods as your counselors; and afterwards, when any counsel is given you, remember what counselors you have assumed, and whose advice you will neglect if you disobey.
enchiridion_section-32.plainEnglish: When you go to a fortune-teller, remember this: you don't know what will happen, and that's what you're asking about. But you already know what kind of thing it is — if you think like a philosopher. If it's something outside your control, it can't be truly good or bad for you. So don't bring hope or fear to the fortune-teller. Don't go there shaking with worry. First understand clearly that whatever happens doesn't really matter to you. It's neutral. Because you'll always have the power to respond well to it, and no one can take that away from you. Then go confidently to the gods for advice. And when they give you guidance, remember who you asked for help. Remember whose advice you're ignoring if you don't follow it.

enchiridion_section-32.originalText: Come to divination as Socrates prescribed, in cases of which the whole consideration relates to the event, and in which no opportunities are afforded by reason or any other art to discover the matter in view. When, therefore, it is our duty to share the danger of a friend or of our country, we ought not to consult the oracle as to whether we shall share it with them or not. For though the diviner should forewarn you that the auspices are unfavorable, this means no more than that either death or mutilation or exile is portended. But we have reason within us; and it directs us, even with these hazards, to stand by our friend and our country. Attend, therefore, to the greater diviner, the Pythian God, who once cast out of the temple him who neglected to save his friend.
enchiridion_section-32.plainEnglish: Use divination the way Socrates said to. Only when the whole question is about what will happen, and you can't figure it out through reason or any other skill. So when it's your duty to share danger with a friend or your country, don't ask an oracle whether you should do it or not. Even if the fortune-teller warns you that the signs are bad — meaning death, injury, or exile might be coming — so what? You have reason inside you. And reason tells you to stand by your friend and country, even with those risks. Listen to the greater fortune-teller: Apollo himself. He once threw someone out of his temple for failing to save his friend.

enchiridion_section-33.originalText:
Begin by prescribing to yourself some character and demeanor, such as you may preserve both alone and in company.

Be mostly silent, or speak merely what is needful, and in few words. We may, however, enter sparingly into discourse sometimes, when occasion calls for it; but let it not run on any of the common subjects, as gladiators, or horse races, or athletic champions, or food, or drink—the vulgar topics of conversation—and especially not on men, so as either to blame, or praise, or make comparisons. If you are able, then, by your own conversation, bring over that of your company to proper subjects; but if you happen to find yourself among strangers, be silent.

Let not your laughter be loud, frequent, or abundant.
enchiridion_section-33.plainEnglish:
First, decide what kind of person you want to be. Then stick to that character whether you're alone or with others.

Stay quiet most of the time. When you do speak, say only what's necessary and keep it brief. You can join conversations occasionally when it makes sense, but don't let them drift into common topics like sports, celebrities, food, or drinks — the usual shallow stuff people talk about. And especially don't gossip about people — whether you're criticizing them, praising them, or comparing them. If you can steer the conversation toward better topics, do it. But if you're stuck with strangers, just stay quiet.

Don't laugh too loud, too often, or too much.

enchiridion_section-33.originalText:
Avoid taking oaths, if possible, altogether; at any rate, so far as you are able.

Avoid public and vulgar entertainments; but if ever an occasion calls you to them, keep your attention upon the stretch, that you may not imperceptibly slide into vulgarity. For be assured that if a person be ever so pure himself, yet, if his companion be corrupted, he who converses with him will be corrupted likewise.
enchiridion_section-33.plainEnglish:
Don't make promises or swear oaths if you can help it. At least avoid them as much as possible.

Stay away from cheap, popular entertainment. But if you must go, stay alert. Don't let yourself slip into being crude without noticing. Remember this: even if you're a good person, spending time with corrupt people will corrupt you too.

enchiridion_section-33.originalText:
Provide things relating to the body no further than absolute need requires, as meat, drink, clothing, house, retinue. But cut off everything that looks toward show and luxury.

Before marriage guard yourself with all your ability from unlawful intercourse with women; yet be not uncharitable or severe to those who are led into this, nor boast frequently that you yourself do otherwise.
enchiridion_section-33.plainEnglish:
Only give your body what it absolutely needs: food, water, clothes, shelter, basic help from others. Cut out anything that's just for show or luxury.

Before you get married, do everything you can to avoid sleeping with women. But don't be harsh or judgmental toward people who do this. And don't brag about how you're better than them.

enchiridion_section-33.originalText: If anyone tells you that a certain person speaks ill of you, do not make excuses about what is said of you, but answer: "He was ignorant of my other faults, else he would not have mentioned these alone."
enchiridion_section-33.plainEnglish: If someone tells you that a person spoke badly about you, don't defend yourself against what they said. Instead, respond: "He doesn't know about my other flaws, or he wouldn't have mentioned just those ones."

enchiridion_section-33.originalText: It is not necessary for you to appear often at public spectacles; but if ever there is a proper occasion for you to be there, do not appear more solicitous for any other than for yourself—that is, wish things to be only just as they are, and only the best man to win; for thus nothing will go against you. But abstain entirely from acclamations and derision and violent emotions. And when you come away, do not discourse a great deal on what has passed and what contributes nothing to your own amendment. For it would appear by such discourse that you were dazzled by the show.
enchiridion_section-33.plainEnglish: You don't need to go to public events very often. But when you do go, don't care more about anyone else than yourself. Want things to happen exactly as they do. Want the best person to win. This way, nothing will upset you. Don't cheer loudly, don't mock anyone, and don't get worked up. When you leave, don't spend a lot of time talking about what happened if it doesn't help you improve yourself. All that chatter just shows the spectacle impressed you too much.

enchiridion_section-33.originalText:
Be not prompt or ready to attend private recitations; but if you do attend, preserve your gravity and dignity, and yet avoid making yourself disagreeable.

When you are going to confer with anyone, and especially with one who seems your superior, represent to yourself how Socrates or Zeno would behave in such a case, and you will not be at a loss to meet properly whatever may occur.
enchiridion_section-33.plainEnglish:
Don't be eager to attend private readings and performances. But if you do go, stay serious and dignified. Just don't make yourself unpleasant.

When you're about to meet with someone — especially someone who seems above you — ask yourself how Socrates or Zeno would handle it. Then you'll know how to act, no matter what happens.

enchiridion_section-33.originalText: When you are going before anyone in power, fancy to yourself that you may not find him at home, that you may be shut out, that the doors may not be opened to you, that he may not notice you. If, with all this, it be your duty to go, bear what happens and never say to yourself, "It was not worth so much"; for this is vulgar, and like a man bewildered by externals.
enchiridion_section-33.plainEnglish: When you're going to meet someone in power, imagine ahead of time that they might not be home. You might be turned away. The doors might stay locked. They might ignore you completely. If you still have a duty to go, then go. Accept whatever happens. Never tell yourself afterward, "That wasn't worth the trouble." That kind of thinking is shallow. It shows you're confused about what really matters.

enchiridion_section-33.originalText: In company, avoid a frequent and excessive mention of your own actions and dangers. For however agreeable it may be to yourself to allude to the risks you have run, it is not equally agreeable to others to hear your adventures. Avoid likewise an endeavor to excite laughter, for this may readily slide you into vulgarity, and, besides, may be apt to lower you in the esteem of your acquaintance. Approaches to indecent discourse are likewise dangerous. Therefore, when anything of this sort happens, use the first fit opportunity to rebuke him who makes advances that way, or, at least, by silence and blushing and a serious look show yourself to be displeased by such talk.
enchiridion_section-33.plainEnglish: When you're with other people, don't constantly talk about your own accomplishments and close calls. Sure, you might enjoy reliving your exciting moments, but others don't want to hear your war stories all the time. Also avoid trying too hard to make people laugh. This can easily make you look cheap, and it might make people respect you less. Stay away from dirty jokes and inappropriate conversations too. When someone starts going down that path, speak up and tell them to stop. Or at least show your disapproval by staying quiet, looking embarrassed, and keeping a serious expression.

enchiridion_section-34.originalText:
If you are dazzled by the semblance of any promised pleasure, guard
yourself against being bewildered by it; but let the affair wait your
leisure, and procure yourself some delay. Then bring to your mind both
points of time—that in which you shall enjoy the pleasure, and that in
which you will repent and reproach yourself, after you have enjoyed
it—and set before you, in opposition to these, how you will rejoice and
applaud yourself if you abstain. And even though it should appear to you
a seasonable gratification, take heed that its enticements and
allurements and seductions may not subdue you, but set in opposition to
this how much better it is to be conscious of having gained so great a
victory.
enchiridion_section-34.plainEnglish: When some pleasure tempts you, don't let it fool you. Take your time. Don't rush into it. Think about two moments: the moment you'll enjoy the pleasure, and the moment afterward when you'll regret it and feel bad about yourself. Compare these to how good you'll feel if you say no. Even if the pleasure seems harmless and well-timed, don't let it seduce you. Remember how much better it feels to win this kind of victory over yourself.

enchiridion_section-35.originalText:
When you do anything from a clear judgment that it ought to be done,
never shrink from being seen to do it, even though the world should
misunderstand it; for if you are not acting rightly, shun the action
itself; if you are, why fear those who wrongly censure you?
enchiridion_section-35.plainEnglish: When you decide something is right and you need to do it, don't hide from doing it just because people might misunderstand. If what you're doing is wrong, then don't do it at all. But if it's right, why worry about people who criticize you unfairly?

enchiridion_section-36.originalText:
As the proposition, “either it is day or it is night,” has much force in
a disjunctive argument, but none at all in a conjunctive one, so, at a
feast, to choose the largest share is very suitable to the bodily
appetite, but utterly inconsistent with the social spirit of the
entertainment. Remember, then, when you eat with another, not only the
value to the body of those things which are set before you, but also the
value of proper courtesy toward your host.
enchiridion_section-36.plainEnglish: Just like the statement "either it is day or it is night" works well in one type of logical argument but not another, grabbing the biggest portion at a dinner party might satisfy your hunger but completely ruins the social purpose of the meal. So when you eat with others, don't just think about how the food will benefit your body. Also think about showing proper respect to your host.

enchiridion_section-37.originalText:
If you have assumed any character beyond your strength, you have both
demeaned yourself ill in that and quitted one which you might have
supported.
enchiridion_section-37.plainEnglish: If you try to play a role that's too big for you, you mess up twice. You do badly at the role you can't handle. And you abandon a role you actually could have done well.

enchiridion_section-38.originalText:
As in walking you take care not to tread upon a nail, or turn your foot,
so likewise take care not to hurt the ruling faculty of your mind. And if
we were to guard against this in every action, we should enter upon
action more safely.
enchiridion_section-38.plainEnglish: When you walk, you watch out for nails and uneven ground so you don't hurt your foot. Do the same with your mind — protect your ability to think clearly. If you guard your mind in everything you do, you'll act more safely.

enchiridion_section-39.originalText:
The body is to everyone the proper measure of its possessions, as the
foot is of the shoe. If, therefore, you stop at this, you will keep the
measure; but if you move beyond it, you must necessarily be carried
forward, as down a precipice; as in the case of a shoe, if you go beyond
its fitness to the foot, it comes first to be gilded, then purple, and
then studded with jewels. For to that which once exceeds the fit measure
there is no bound.
enchiridion_section-39.plainEnglish: The body sets the right limit for what you need to own, just like your foot sets the right size for your shoe. If you stick to this limit, you'll stay balanced. But if you go beyond it, you'll get carried away like falling off a cliff. Think about shoes: once you stop caring if they fit your foot properly, first you want them gold-plated, then purple, then covered in jewels. Once you abandon the right measure, there's no limit to how far you'll go.

enchiridion_section-40.originalText:
Women from fourteen years old are flattered by men with the title of
mistresses. Therefore, perceiving that they are regarded only as
qualified to give men pleasure, they begin to adorn themselves, and in
that to place all their hopes. It is worth while, therefore, to try that
they may perceive themselves honored only so far as they appear beautiful
in their demeanor and modestly virtuous.
enchiridion_section-40.plainEnglish: Men start calling women "mistresses" when they're just fourteen years old. Women notice that men only see them as sources of pleasure. So they focus all their energy on making themselves attractive. That's where they put all their hopes. We should help them understand something better: they deserve honor for how they conduct themselves and for being genuinely virtuous, not just for looking good.

enchiridion_section-41.originalText:
It is a mark of want of intellect to spend much time in things relating
to the body, as to be immoderate in exercises, in eating and drinking,
and in the discharge of other animal functions. These things should be
done incidentally and our main strength be applied to our reason.
enchiridion_section-41.plainEnglish: It shows a lack of intelligence to spend too much time on physical things. Don't overdo exercise, eating, drinking, or other bodily functions. Handle these things quickly and put your main energy into developing your mind.

enchiridion_section-42.originalText:
When any person does ill by you, or speaks ill of you, remember that he
acts or speaks from an impression that it is right for him to do so. Now
it is not possible that he should follow what appears right to you, but
only what appears so to himself. Therefore, if he judges from false
appearances, he is the person hurt, since he, too, is the person
deceived. For if anyone takes a true proposition to be false, the
proposition is not hurt, but only the man is deceived. Setting out, then,
from these principles, you will meekly bear with a person who reviles
you, for you will say upon every occasion, “It seemed so to him.”
enchiridion_section-42.plainEnglish: When someone wrongs you or insults you, remember this: they're acting based on what they think is right. They can't follow what seems right to you — only what seems right to them. So if they're judging from false impressions, they're the one getting hurt. They're the one being deceived. Think of it this way: if someone believes a true statement is false, the statement isn't damaged — only the person is confused. Keep these ideas in mind. Then you can handle insults calmly. You'll just say to yourself, "That's how it seemed to them."

enchiridion_section-43.originalText:
Everything has two handles: one by which it may be borne, another by
which it cannot. If your brother acts unjustly, do not lay hold on the
affair by the handle of his injustice, for by that it cannot be borne,
but rather by the opposite—that he is your brother, that he was brought
up with you; and thus you will lay hold on it as it is to be borne.
enchiridion_section-43.plainEnglish: Everything has two handles: one you can carry it by, one you can't. If your brother treats you unfairly, don't grab the situation by the handle of his unfairness — you can't carry it that way. Instead, grab it by the other handle — that he's your brother, that you grew up together. That's how you can carry it.

enchiridion_section-44.originalText:
These reasonings have no logical connection: “I am richer than you,
therefore I am your superior.” “I am more eloquent than you, therefore I
am your superior.” The true logical connection is rather this: “I am
richer than you, therefore my possessions must exceed yours.” “I am more
eloquent than you, therefore my style must surpass yours.” But you, after
all, consist neither in property nor in style.
enchiridion_section-44.plainEnglish: These arguments make no sense: "I have more money than you, so I'm better than you." "I speak better than you, so I'm better than you." Here's what actually follows logically: "I have more money than you, so my possessions are worth more than yours." "I speak better than you, so my speaking style is better than yours." But you as a person are not your possessions or your speaking style.

enchiridion_section-45.originalText:
Does anyone bathe hastily? Do not say that he does it ill, but hastily.
Does anyone drink much wine? Do not say that he does ill, but that he
drinks a great deal. For unless you perfectly understand his motives, how
should you know if he acts ill? Thus you will not risk yielding to any
appearances but such as you fully comprehend.
enchiridion_section-45.plainEnglish: Does someone take a quick bath? Don't say they're doing it wrong — just say they're doing it quickly. Does someone drink a lot of wine? Don't say they're doing something bad — just say they drink a lot. Unless you completely understand why they're acting that way, how can you know if they're actually doing something wrong? This way, you won't jump to conclusions about things you don't fully understand.

enchiridion_section-46.originalText:
Never proclaim yourself a philosopher, nor make much talk among the
ignorant about your principles, but show them by actions. Thus, at an
entertainment, do not discourse how people ought to eat, but eat as you
ought. For remember that thus Socrates also universally avoided all
ostentation. And when persons came to him and desired to be introduced by
him to philosophers, he took them and introduced them; so well did he
bear being overlooked. So if ever there should be among the ignorant any
discussion of principles, be for the most part silent. For there is great
danger in hastily throwing out what is undigested. And if anyone tells
you that you know nothing, and you are not nettled at it, then you may be
sure that you have really entered on your work. For sheep do not hastily
throw up the grass to show the shepherds how much they have eaten, but,
inwardly digesting their food, they produce it outwardly in wool and
milk. Thus, therefore, do you not make an exhibition before the ignorant
of your principles, but of the actions to which their digestion gives
rise.
enchiridion_section-46.plainEnglish: Don't call yourself a philosopher. Don't talk endlessly about your principles to people who won't understand. Show them through your actions instead. At a dinner party, don't lecture people about how they should eat. Just eat properly yourself. Remember, Socrates avoided showing off too. When people asked him to introduce them to philosophers, he quietly took them and made the introductions. He handled being ignored really well. So if ignorant people start discussing principles, stay mostly quiet. It's dangerous to blurt out half-baked ideas. And if someone says you know nothing and it doesn't bother you, then you know you're on the right track. Sheep don't throw up grass to show shepherds how much they've eaten. Instead, they digest it quietly and produce wool and milk. Do the same thing. Don't show off your principles to ignorant people. Show them the actions that come from truly understanding those principles.

enchiridion_section-47.originalText:
When you have learned to nourish your body frugally, do not pique
yourself upon it; nor, if you drink water, be saying upon every occasion,
“I drink water.” But first consider how much more frugal are the poor
than we, and how much more patient of hardship. If at any time you would
inure yourself by exercise to labor and privation, for your own sake and
not for the public, do not attempt great feats; but when you are
violently thirsty, just rinse your mouth with water, and tell nobody.
enchiridion_section-47.plainEnglish: When you learn to live simply and eat less, don't brag about it. If you drink water instead of wine, don't announce it every chance you get. First, think about how much simpler the poor live than we do. Think about how much hardship they endure. If you want to train yourself to handle hard work and going without things, do it for yourself, not to impress others. Don't try anything extreme. When you're really thirsty, just rinse your mouth with water and don't tell anyone about it.

enchiridion_section-48.originalText:
The condition and characteristic of a vulgar person is that he never
looks for either help or harm from himself, but only from externals. The
condition and characteristic of a philosopher is that he looks to himself
for all help or harm. The marks of a proficient are that he censures no
one, praises no one, blames no one, accuses no one; says nothing
concerning himself as being anybody or knowing anything. When he is in
any instance hindered or restrained, he accuses himself; and if he is
praised, he smiles to himself at the person who praises him; and if he is
censured, he makes no defense. But he goes about with the caution of a
convalescent, careful of interference with anything that is doing well
but not yet quite secure. He restrains desire; he transfers his aversion
to those things only which thwart the proper use of our own will; he
employs his energies moderately in all directions; if he appears stupid
or ignorant, he does not care; and, in a word, he keeps watch over
himself as over an enemy and one in ambush.
enchiridion_section-48.plainEnglish: An ordinary person always looks outside himself for help or harm. A philosopher looks only to himself for help or harm. Here are the signs of someone making real progress: He doesn't criticize anyone, praise anyone, blame anyone, or accuse anyone. He doesn't talk about himself like he's important or knowledgeable. When something blocks him or holds him back, he blames himself. If someone praises him, he quietly smiles at that person. If someone criticizes him, he doesn't argue back. He moves carefully, like someone recovering from an illness. He's cautious about messing with anything that's going well but isn't secure yet. He controls his desires. He only dislikes things that interfere with using his own will properly. He uses his energy moderately in everything. If he seems stupid or ignorant, he doesn't care. In short, he watches himself like he's watching an enemy lying in wait.

enchiridion_section-49.originalText:
When anyone shows himself vain on being able to understand and interpret
the works of Chrysippus,[7] say to yourself: “Unless Chrysippus had
written obscurely, this person would have had nothing to be vain of. But
what do I desire? To understand nature, and follow her. I ask, then, who
interprets her; and hearing that Chrysippus does, I have recourse to him.
I do not understand his writings. I seek, therefore, one to interpret
_them_.” So far there is nothing to value myself upon. And when I find an
interpreter, what remains is to make use of his instructions. This alone
is the valuable thing. But if I admire merely the interpretation, what do
I become more than a grammarian, instead of a philosopher, except,
indeed, that instead of Homer I interpret Chrysippus? When anyone,
therefore, desires me to read Chrysippus to him, I rather blush when I
cannot exhibit actions that are harmonious and consonant with his
discourse.
enchiridion_section-49.plainEnglish: When someone brags about understanding Chrysippus's complicated philosophy, tell yourself this: "If Chrysippus had written clearly, this person would have nothing to brag about. But what do I actually want? To understand nature and live by it. I ask who can teach me this. People say Chrysippus can, so I turn to him. I don't understand his writings. So I look for someone to explain them." Nothing impressive so far. When I find someone to explain his ideas, what matters next is actually using those lessons. That's the only valuable part. If I just admire clever interpretations, I'm no better than a literature teacher instead of a philosopher. The only difference is I'm analyzing Chrysippus instead of Homer. So when someone asks me to explain Chrysippus to them, I feel embarrassed when my actions don't match up with his teachings.

enchiridion_section-50.originalText: Whatever rules you have adopted, abide by them as laws, and as if you would be impious to transgress them; and do not regard what anyone says of you, for this, after all, is no concern of yours.
enchiridion_section-50.plainEnglish: Whatever rules you've chosen to live by, stick to them like laws. Act as if breaking them would be a sin. Don't worry about what people say about you. That's not your business anyway.

enchiridion_section-50.originalText: How long, then, will you delay to demand of yourself the noblest improvements, and in no instance to transgress the judgments of reason? You have received the philosophic principles with which you ought to be conversant; and you have been conversant with them. For what other master, then, do you wait as an excuse for this delay in self-reformation? You are no longer a boy but a grown man. If, therefore, you will be negligent and slothful, and always add procrastination to procrastination, purpose to purpose, and fix day after day in which you will attend to yourself, you will insensibly continue to accomplish nothing and, living and dying, remain of vulgar mind.
enchiridion_section-50.plainEnglish: How long will you keep putting off becoming your best self? How long will you ignore what reason tells you to do? You already know the philosophical principles you need. You've studied them. What teacher are you waiting for? What excuse do you need? You're not a kid anymore. You're a grown adult. If you keep being lazy and careless, if you keep saying 'I'll start tomorrow' and 'I'll do it next week,' if you keep setting dates to work on yourself but never follow through, you'll accomplish nothing. You'll live an ordinary life and die with an ordinary mind.

enchiridion_section-50.originalText: This instant, then, think yourself worthy of living as a man grown up and a proficient. Let whatever appears to be the best be to you an inviolable law. And if any instance of pain or pleasure, glory or disgrace, be set before you, remember that now is the combat, now the Olympiad comes on, nor can it be put off; and that by one failure and defeat honor may be lost or—won. Thus Socrates became perfect, improving himself by everything, following reason alone. And though you are not yet a Socrates, you ought, however, to live as one seeking to be a Socrates.
enchiridion_section-50.plainEnglish: Right now, think of yourself as a grown adult and someone who's getting good at this. Whatever seems like the best choice — treat it like an unbreakable rule. When pain or pleasure, praise or shame comes your way, remember that this is the fight. This is your Olympics. You can't postpone it. One failure or victory can lose or win you everything. This is how Socrates became perfect. He learned from everything and followed reason alone. You're not Socrates yet. But you should live like someone who's trying to become him.

enchiridion_section-51.originalText: The first and most necessary topic in philosophy is the practical application of principles, as, _We ought not to lie_; the second is that of demonstrations as, _Why it is that we ought not to lie_; the third, that which gives strength and logical connection to the other two, as, _Why this is a demonstration_. For what is demonstration? What is a consequence? What a contradiction? What truth? What falsehood? The third point is then necessary on account of the second; and the second on account of the first. But the most necessary, and that whereon we ought to rest, is the first. But we do just the contrary. For we spend all our time on the third point and employ all our diligence about that, and entirely neglect the first. Therefore, at the same time that we lie, we are very ready to show how it is demonstrated that lying is wrong.
enchiridion_section-51.plainEnglish: Philosophy has three levels. First: practicing principles like "don't lie." Second: understanding why — "here's why you shouldn't lie." Third: understanding the logic itself — "here's why this proof works." What is proof? What follows from what? What's a contradiction? What's true or false? The third level supports the second. The second supports the first. The most important level — the one we should focus on — is the first. But we do the opposite. We spend all our time on the third level. We work hard to understand logic and theory. We completely ignore the first level. So we lie while being ready to prove that lying is wrong.

enchiridion_section-51.originalText:
Upon all occasions we ought to have these maxims ready at hand:

Conduct me, Zeus, and thou, O Destiny,
Wherever your decrees have fixed my lot.
I follow cheerfully; and, did I not,
Wicked and wretched, I must follow still.[8]

Who'er yields properly to Fate is deemed
Wise among men, and knows the laws of Heaven.[9]

And this third:

"O Crito, if it thus pleases the gods, thus let it be."[10]

"Anytus and Melitus may kill me indeed; but hurt me they cannot."[11]
enchiridion_section-51.plainEnglish:
Keep these sayings ready for any situation:

"Lead me, Zeus, and you, Destiny, wherever you have decided my path should go. I'll follow willingly. And if I don't want to follow, I'll still have to — but then I'd be miserable and wrong."

"Anyone who accepts fate properly is considered wise and understands how the universe works."

And this third one:

"Crito, if this is what the gods want, then let it be."

"Anytus and Melitus can kill me, but they cannot truly harm me."
